articles.content:

                        Norwegian citizenship comes with a hefty application fee and plenty of requirements. There are several reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration might reject an application.

Lifetime enrollment in the Norwegian National Insurance Scheme, the ability to live in Norway for as long as you wish, and returning to Norway after a few years away without going through the immigration process are some of the many benefits of Norwegian citizenship.

Norwegian citizenship doesn’t come easy, though. In addition to waiting years to become eligible, you will have to pass language and citizenship tests, provide a criminal record certificate, verify your identity and meet the requirements for permanent residence if you don’t hold it already.

This is all before you pay 6,500 kroner to apply for Norwegian citizenship.

So, what are the reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) turns down applications?

This applies not just to your citizenship application but also to your entire stay. If you bend the rules when it comes to the residence requirements, you could find your citizenship application rejected.

Even if your application is successful, you will find your citizenship revoked later if the UDI finds out. The UDI will still revoke your citizenship, even if you are the one who decides to come clean to them.

Should the authorities have reason to believe that you have provided incorrect information on any residence or citizenship applications, they will typically invite you for an interview with the police or notify you of your revocation in advance.

READ MORE: How Norway can revoke residency and citizenship over wrong details

This one might seem obvious, but it can happen relatively easily. One of the most common reasons for a foreign national having their citizenship rejected is not passing the citizenship or social studies test (in Norwegian).

For the citizenship test, you must answer 24 out of 36 multiple-choice questions correctly.

The social studies test is taken by those who typically have been through the social studies course for immigrants.

Language-wise, you will generally have to have passed an oral test in Norwegian at  B1 level.

Another common pitfall is the criminal record certificate. Criminal record certificates are only valid for three months. The certification proves that you haven’t been convicted of any crimes and are not disqualified from applying for citizenship.

As the certificate can only be valid for three months, the UDI advises that you shouldn’t order the certificate until you have an appointment to hand in your documents to the police. This reduces the likelihood of the certificate expiring before your documents are handed in.

Failure to meet any of the citizenship requirements will result in your application being turned down. You must also hold a valid residence permit whilst applying for citizenship.

Remember that under standard rules, you must have stayed in Norway for a total of eight of the past eleven years and held residence permits that were each valid for at least one year.

On the UDI website, you can learn how to calculate residence periods in exception cases. However, as there is currently a proposal to amend the Citizenship Act, which could alter how qualifying residence time is measured, these requirements may change in the future.

READ MORE: What will Norway's plan to toughen citizenship rules mean for you?

Being convicted of a criminal offence that results in a fine or prison sentence will bar you from being eligible for citizenship for a set period of time.

The disqualification period can range from 2.5 years up to 39 years, depending on the severity of your punishment. You can see an overview of the disqualification rules on the UDI website.

Those who have received fixed penalty notices rather than criminal fines will not be disqualified. Those who have had charges or cases dropped are also not disqualified.

An example of a fixed penalty notice would be a fine for minor or moderate speeding.

To be eligible for citizenship, you also need to be eligible for permanent residence at the same time, which can make matters confusing.

For many, the easiest way around this is to just hold permanent residence as proof of eligibility while applying for citizenship.

The key thing to look out for when it comes to citizenship is the minimum income requirements for non-EEA permanent residence applicants.

One of the requirements for permanent residence applications for non-EEA nationals is that you will need to have fulfilled the income requirements for the previous 12 months and that you cannot have received financial assistance (økonomisk sosialhjelp) during the prior 12 months.

articles.title: Frøhvelvet på Svalbard får pris
articles.content:
Det globale frøhvelvet på Svalbard mottok i dag Fyrstinne av Asturias-prisen for internasjonalt samarbeid.

Prisutdelingen foregikk i Spania med den spanske kongefamilien til stede, og landbruks- og matminister Nils Kristen Sandtrøen tok imot prisen på vegne av det norske frøhvelvet.

Frøhvelvet hedres for sitt bidrag til internasjonalt samarbeid og langsiktig sikring av verdens mangfold av nytteplanter.

Så langt er det deponert 1,4 millioner frøprøver lagret i hvelvet.

Klima og miljø

Verden opplever allerede klimaendringene, slår FNs klimapanel fast. Mer ekstremvær, høyere havnivå og økte helseproblemer er noen av konsekvensene, ifølge deres siste hovedrapport.

                        Norway's sovereign wealth fund, the world's largest with assets of more than $2 trillion, on Thursday reported a negative return of 278 billion kroner ($31 billion) in the third quarter as it was weighed down by higher interest rates.

It posted a negative return of 0.5 percent in the quarter, dragged down by a negative return of 3.5 percent in its fixed-income investments, while its equity and property portfolios increased by 0.5 percent and 0.4 percent respectively.

"The fund's return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments," the fund's deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement.

Invested primarily in equities, bonds and real estate across the globe, the fund reported a value of 22,014 billion kroner at the end of September.

Inflation around the world, fuelled in particular by soaring energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East, has led several central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, to raise interest rates in the third quarter.

"Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell," Grande said.

Fuelled by the Nordic country's oil revenues, the fund is invested in more than 7,100 companies spanning the globe, and holds around 1.5 percent of all listed companies worldwide, making it the world's largest single investor.

articles.title: IN DATA: Who were the 5,000 foreigners deported from Norway last year?
articles.content:
Add a comment
                                                                                            
                                        
                                                                        
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                
                            
                        
                    
                    
                    
                            
                            In 2025, Norwegian authorities issued formal deportation orders (utvisningsvedtak) to 5,002 foreign nationals. Photo by Blake Guidry on Unsplash
                    
                                            
                            
        
            
            
            
            
        
        Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        As well as tracking how many people move to Norway, the Directorate of Immigration (UDI) also monitors foreign nationals ordered to leave the country (with British citizens throwing up a surprise).

In 2025, Norwegian authorities issued formal deportation orders (utvisningsvedtak) to 5,002 foreign nationals, according to statistics from UDI.

A deportation order in Norway carries a formal entry ban, which prevents the person from returning to Norway for a certain period, or permanently in serious cases. It can even include a ban from entering the Schengen Area.

One of the main reasons a foreign resident can be deported from Norway is breaking the Immigration Act. This includes administrative violations like overstaying a visa, working without a valid permit, giving false information on residency applications, or not leaving the country after an asylum or visa refusal.

In 2025, 4,125 orders (which represents 82.5 percent of the total deportation orders) were issued on these grounds.

Foreign nationals can also be expelled from Norway after a criminal conviction, but this is much less common. Last year there were 368 such cases (7.4 percent of all deportation orders).

Contrary to popular belief, EU citizens are not exempt from being expelled from Norway, even though they have freedom of movement under the EEA Agreement.

In 2025, 500 orders (10 percent of all cases) were issued to European nationals. This can happen on grounds such as public order, public security, or abuse of rights.

In 2025, most deportation orders were given to nationals from South Asia and West Africa.

India had the highest number of cases with 949 in total. Of these, 941 were for immigration breaches and eight for criminal convictions. Pakistan was next with 918 orders, 917 for immigration breaches and one for a criminal conviction.

There was then a sharp drop. Bangladesh came third with 331 orders (329 for immigration breaches and two for criminal offences), and Nigeria in fourth place with 227 orders (218 for immigration breaches and nine for criminal convictions).

Combined, nationals from these four countries made up nearly 49 percent of all deportation orders in Norway in 2025.

Further down the overall list among non-EEA states were countries like Kenya with 112, Nepal (139), Ghana (111), China (78), the UK (62), Ukraine (59), and the United States with 42.

Australia and Canada recorded just 8 and 10 orders, respectively.

Among the European nationals, the highest number of expulsion orders was issued to citizens from Romania (160), Lithuania (89), Poland (75), and neighbouring Sweden (64), followed by the Netherlands (20), Latvia (13), and Spain (12).

UK nationals top list of convicted criminals deported

The figures show an unexpected trend in criminal deportations. Of the 62 British citizens ordered to leave in 2025, 35 were deported after criminal convictions. This made the UK the country with the most convicted criminals deported from Norway last year, ahead of Ukraine (33), China (31), and the United States (19).

A further 25 Britons were expelled for immigration status violations after losing EU freedom of movement post-Brexit.

READ ALSO: Indians, Brits and Syrians top Norway's permanent residency list

UDI statistics show a steady increase in expulsions in recent years.

Norwegian authorities recorded 1,210 deportation orders in 2021, 1,894 in 2022, 2,893 in 2023, and 3,302 in 2024. With the total passing the 5,000 mark in 2025, expulsion orders were more than four times higher than four years prior.

articles.content:
Minst seks personer er drept og 28 er såret etter at væpnede menn åpnet ild under en begravelse i en kirke sør i Jordan, opplyser en talsperson for regjeringen til nyhetsbyrået AP.

Den statlige TV-kanalen Al-Mamlaka melder at to menn skal ha kommet ut av et kjøretøy og begynt å skyte i en gresk-ortodoks kirke i Karak fredag ettermiddag.

Karak huser en kristen minoritetsbefolkning og ligger rundt 180 kilometer sør for Jordans hovedstad Amman.

Khaled Burqan, som deltok i begravelsen, fortalte at en av mennene hadde et gevær og den andre en pistol og at de skjøt mot menneskene i kirken i flere minutter.

Det er ikke kjent hvem som står bak angrepet. Politiets sikkerhetsstyrker rykket ut til åstedet og tok opp jakten på gjerningsmennene fredag ettermiddag.

articles.content:
Det er sendt ut oransje farevarsel om flaum for store delar av Austlandet aust for Oslo, ifølge Varsom.no.

articles.title: Today in Norway: A roundup of the latest news on Friday
articles.content:
Add a comment
                                                                                            
                                        
                                                                        
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                
                            
                        
                    
                    
                    
                            
                            Libe Rieber-Mohn, Director of the Norwegian Directorate for Integration and Diversity (IMDi). Photo: Erik Thallaug / IMDi
                    
                                            
                            
        
            
            
            
            
        
        Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Norway expects almost 2,000 fewer refugees next year, details from the Storting gala dinner and King Haakon's speech, and more news on Friday.

Almost 2,000 fewer refugees expected in Norway next year

This marks the lowest expected number since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Norwegian municipalities have resettled over 110,000 refugees, most of whom came from Ukraine.

"There has been a marked decline in recent years, but from a historically high level. The number to be resettled next year is still significant in a Norwegian context," said Libe Rieber-Mohn, director of IMDi.​

Minister of Labour and Social Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng also explained in a statement: "The Labour Party government has taken a number of steps to limit the number of displaced people coming to Norway. We are now seeing the results of that. We will not accept more than we can integrate, while continuing to stand up for Ukraine and ensure a safe stay for displaced people in Norway."

The ministry said that several municipalities are experiencing pressure on housing markets and local public services (such as schools, kindergartens, and health and care facilities) following several years of high settlement numbers. Authorities also pointed out that secondary migration is an issue, as refugees sometimes move away from the municipality where they first settled.

​In response, officials are introducing tighter criteria for resettlement requests next year, which they say will help with integration and prevent segregation.

"The government has changed the criteria for requests to avoid settling refugees in areas with big challenges and to make it easier to find work quickly. Because of this, municipalities like Fredrikstad, Sarpsborg, and Halden will not be asked to settle refugees in 2027," Stenseng said.

Daily smoking falls in Norway, especially among Gen Z

In its latest survey on tobacco, alcohol, and substance use, Statistics Norway (SSB) reported that daily cigarette smoking has dropped to 6 percent, down from 7 percent last year. Meanwhile, daily use of snus, the small nicotine pouches, remains more than twice as common at 15 percent, reaching 22 percent among men.

"Over the past 10 years, there have been changes in the population's tobacco habits, and there are now more than twice as many daily users of snus compared to daily smokers," said Sindre Mikael Haugen, a senior adviser at Statistics Norway, in an accompanying article.

The agency also pointed out a clear generational divide in tobacco use as generation Z could be Norway’s first generation with very few daily smokers.

"To use a widely used generational division, one could say that Gen Z (1997–2012) is possibly the first generation without, and Millennials (1981–1996) the last generation with, a significant proportion of people who have smoked daily," Haugen said.

Interestingly, the figures also show that very few people both smoke and use snus every day. This suggests the two habits rarely happen together.

​King Haakon and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra mark historic "firsts" at Storting gala dinner

On Thursday evening, the Royal Palace in Oslo held one of Norway’s most prestigious and high-profile traditions (established in 1906): the annual parliamentary dinner (Stortingsmiddagen), where the monarch invites the 169 members of the Storting, cabinet ministers, and other senior state officials to the Palace.

The evening was a significant milestone for the royal family, as King Haakon hosted the gala for the first time as monarch, while Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra wore her first formal gala dress as Crown Princess.

The King’s speech is always a highlight, mixing thoughts about the nation with a personal touch. King Haakon started his speech by honouring his father, the late King Harald, in a very personal way: "So it's me standing here, not my father. I miss him tonight, and I'm sure I'm not alone. This was his arena. He was, as we know, funny—with apt comments and good timing. And not infrequently, dad jokes."

The King made the audience laugh when he talked about how long he had prepared for the role: "As you probably understand, it's not easy to become king overnight. Then having 35 years of experience as a middle manager in a medium-sized public enterprise comes in handy."

He also thanked Queen Mette-Marit for her support: "And it's important to have good people around you—and I'm lucky in that, because I have the Queen on my team. It gives me security and support."

Looking ahead, the King said: "I've had a fantastic coach in any case. Now it's just a matter of managing my energy well. This is a long-distance race, and I'm aiming for consistent speed and good endurance."

Jens Elmelund Kjeldsen, a professor of rhetoric at the University of Bergen, told newspaper Aftenposten the speech was full of metaphors and called it "a factual defence of constitutional democracy."

If you are curious about what the monarch and politicians ate at such a prestigious national gala, public broadcaster NRK shared the details. Guests were served a four-course menu consisting of crab salad, cheese tart, moose from Sikkilsdalen (hunted by the late King Harald's hunting party), and traditional Norwegian cloudberries for dessert.

Norwegian vocabulary: Stortingsmiddagen - the parliamentary dinner

​Practice grenade found in luggage at Tromsø Airport

Police were called to Tromsø Airport on Thursday afternoon after a grenade was discovered in checked baggage during a routine security screening.

Authorities later said there was no danger to the public as the item was a training grenade, not a real one.

"We need to be completely certain before handling it further, which is why our specialists are assessing it," police told public broadcaster NRK before the item was formally cleared.

The security alert caused some delays at the airport, but things soon returned to normal.

articles.content:
Norsk Hydro kunne vise til vekst både i inntjening og resultater i tredje kvartal, men mindre enn markedet hadde ventet på forhånd.

Dermed er Hydro-aksjen også ned 5–6 prosent på Oslo Børs etter et par timers handel.

Selskapet trekker selv frem at høyere priser på metall og alumina styrker regnskapet. På den andre siden trekker en sterkere krone og økte energikostnader ned totalprestasjonen ned.

Norsk Hydro er Norges nest største bedrift målt etter omsetning, og har 32.000 ansatte i 40 ulike land – 3.500 av dem i Norge.

Norsk Hydro

Norsk Hydro fikk et driftsresultat på 9,7 milliarder kroner i tredje kvartal 2022. Det er 2,5 milliarder mer enn resultatet på 7,2 milliarder kroner i samme kvartal i fjor.
